analysis.one_liner: Raises estate and gift taxes on the largest fortunes and closes trust loopholes used to skip them.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have cut the estate tax exemption from roughly $12.9 million to $3.5 million and taxed estates over $1 billion at 65%, died in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax the largest estates and gifts much more heavily: it cuts the tax-free estate amount to $3.5 million, adds a 65% rate on estates over $1 billion, and shuts down common trust and valuation tricks that let the wealthiest families pass money to grandchildren with little or no tax. It also increases protections for family farms and land donors, raising the special farmland valuation to $3 million and doubling the conservation easement exclusion to $2 million. The bill never got a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 99.5% of families whose estates fall below the new $3.5 million threshold would pay no more, while the tax burden shifts onto the largest fortunes and dynasty trusts. Ordinary taxpayers gain indirectly if the added revenue reduces pressure to cut public programs or raise other taxes. Family farms and ranches get extra protection: the amount of farmland value that can be excluded rises from $750,000 to $3 million with inflation adjustments, and the estate tax exclusion for donated conservation easements rises from $500,000 to $2 million at a 60% rate [S2] [S3]. Heirs also gain from new transparency rules requiring the value of inherited or gifted interests to be disclosed to recipients and to Treasury [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families below the estate tax, especially farm owners

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the estate tax exclusion from about $12.9 million to $3.5 million and adds new rates rising to 65% on estates over $1 billion, so the tax falls on the largest fortunes rather than typical families.

Shuts down estate-tax avoidance tools used by the wealthiest: no more valuation discounts on family-controlled entities, grantor retained annuity trusts must run at least 10 years with a real remainder value, grantor trusts are pulled back into the taxable estate, and the generation-skipping exemption is eliminated for transfers to people more than two generations below the giver.

Expands protections for family farms and working land: the special-use farmland valuation cap rises from $750,000 to $3 million (adjusted for inflation), and the conservation easement estate tax exclusion rises from $500,000 to $2 million at a 60% exclusion rate.

Adds transparency and enforcement rules: estates and large gift filers must report consistent basis and disclose to Treasury and to each recipient the value of every interest received, making it harder to understate inherited wealth.

analysis.who_pays: Estates worth more than $3.5 million, people making large gifts, and creators of dynasty and grantor trusts — concentrated among the wealthiest households. The 65% rate applies only to the slice of estates above $1 billion. Estate-planning professionals lose business as the trust and valuation strategies the bill restricts become unusable.
analysis.who_pays_short: Estates over $3.5 million and dynasty trusts

drawbacks.text: A $3.5 million exemption with rates up to 45% can strain asset-rich but cash-poor family businesses and farms, whose heirs may have to sell assets to pay the tax — though the bill's higher farmland and conservation easement carve-outs are designed to blunt exactly this problem.

The new valuation, trust, and reporting rules (including minimum 10-year trust terms, look-through rules for nonbusiness assets, and per-donor gift limits) add compliance complexity and professional costs for estate administration.
The bill raises revenue but directs it nowhere in particular; it does not pair the new taxes with any spending or tax cut for other taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall almost entirely on the top half of one percent of estates, and the bill specifically cushions family farms and conservation donors, which addresses the most common objection to estate tax increases. The main honest costs are real but modest: complexity in estate administration and some pressure on large family-owned businesses that hold illiquid assets. On balance the gains to the broad taxpaying public outweigh the burdens, which are concentrated on households with millions in wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote, until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jimmy Gomez introduced the bill on April 18, 2023 with 26 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; the action record shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action of any kind afterward.
Cosponsorship grew to 33, every one of them a Democrat, and no version ever advanced.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still stalled in committee, so it died without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy families with large estates and dynasty trusts are better off, since the higher taxes and loophole closures never took effect, and so are estate-planning professionals whose business depends on those strategies.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large estates and the estate-planning industry

for.name: Rep. Jimmy Gomez
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 26 original Democratic cosponsors on day one.

for.name: 33 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Norton, Watson Coleman, Blumenauer, Jayapal, DeLauro, and McGovern

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or committee vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors were House Democrats and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee took no action, so support never crossed party lines.

industries.industry: Ultra-wealthy households and heirs of large estates
industries.note: Estates above $3.5 million would pay sharply more, with a 65% rate on the portion over $1 billion, and dynasty trusts would lose the generation-skipping exemption for distant heirs. Their gain from the bill's defeat was keeping the current exemption above $12 million per person.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory (attorneys, trust companies, GRAT and valuation specialists)
industries.note: The bill's core targets are this industry's products: valuation discounts on family entities, short-term GRATs, sales to grantor trusts, and_entity wrappers around investment assets. Its business model profits from helping clients trim transfer taxes, which runs against the public's interest in taxing concentrated wealth.

industries.industry: Family farms, ranches, and land trusts
industries.note: The bill quadruples the special-use farmland valuation to $3 million and raises the conservation easement exclusion to $2 million at 60%, easing estate taxes on working land and rewarding donated conservation.
